# The ghosts of higher education reform: on the organisational processes surrounding policy borrowing
Katja Brøgger*
Department of Education, Aarhus University, Copenhagen NV, Denmark (Received 28 March 2013; accepted 4 March 2014)
The Bologna Process is one of the most extensive examples of policy borrowing processes. Based on qualitative data, this article argues in favour of studying part of this process as 'global smallness', centring on the organisational effects of the implementation of a globalised curriculum. Through Derrida's notion on hauntology, Fenwick and Edward's analysis of multiple reals, and Barad's understanding of entanglement and time, this article explores how the implementation processes evoke simultaneously existing worlds of practices propelled by the agency of the past troubling present higher education reform. Finally, this article addresses how ongoing reforms tend to increase the stretch between 'what is performed on the outside' and 'what is practiced on the inside'.
Keywords: globalisation; higher education; the Bologna Process as policy borrowing; curriculum; organisational change; hauntology and 'entanglement and time'
## It changes everything: introduction
The Bologna Process is one name – and arguably the most important name – given to the major changes currently being made within higher education, both inside and outside Europe. This process aims to create a European Higher Education Area by transforming the higher education architectures through initiatives and targets such as educational harmonisation, comparability, mobility, flexibility, employability, qualification frameworks and many more. Elena, a lecturer, experiences all of this. In her higher education organisation, a new BA ministerial order and curriculum, shaped in accordance with the European reform processes, is currently being implemented. She says:
You know it's like … Oh, how should I put it? …. Well, I think we experience that … I really don't know how to phrase this … That our entire way of … being an education, being colleagues, our relations with management, our culture is … Well of course it needs to develop all the time; I mean it's not like

we don't move and it's like … but … I currently experience that there are some fundamental relations in our house which are uhm … highly problematic.
Our working conditions and our culture seem so threatened.
This article explores the organisational effects of globalised policy-making. It is based primarily on empirical data from an implementation process of a new educational ministerial order and curriculum, shaped in accordance with the European reform processes at a university and a university college in the nation, but it is also informed by strategic development among managers. This article centres on the effects of two major curricular changes: the shifts towards both modularisation and learning outcomes. The research represents a qualitative study which makes use of observations of top-management meetings, meetings on the revision of the education due to the educational reform (which included participants from mid-level management, lecturers and students), meetings on the development of specific modules (which included only lecturers) and, to a lesser degree, classroom lessons (which included lecturers and students). In addition, the study also refers to email-based logbooks completed by lecturers and mid-level management. Material from both the logbooks and observations was used to prepare interview guidelines for 30 semi-structured interviews. The interviewees were top- and mid-level managers and lecturers. These diverse qualitative methods are combined with document analysis of international and national steering documents related to the Bologna Process, the governmental and institutional level. The empirical data were collected between March 2011 and January 2013 and has been anonymised.
In order to understand the organisational effects of the Bologna Process – i.e., 'global smallness' and how the agency of the past troubles present higher education reform – I bring together ethnographic method, policy studies and poststructuralist philosophy. My contribution aims to establish the impact of globalising reform processes at the organisational level of higher education. To achieve this aim, this article addresses three major challenges in relation to researching today's higher education reform. Firstly, it addresses the methodological challenge of grasping global 'smallness'; in other words, understanding globalising processes at an organisational level. This ambition brings with it profound methodological challenges because it demands that we shake loose globalisation's status as a hegemonic macro-narrative, which often leads to atemporal and ahistorical analyses. It reveals the need to develop a different conceptual language that subverts the global into 'situated smallness'. This article aims to reconceptualise the field by connecting local enactment and international policy processes, and it takes its inspiration from analytical (e.g., Derrida [1987](#page-20-0), [1994,](#page-20-0) [2003](#page-20-0); Dale and Robertson [2012;](#page-19-0) Steiner-Khamsi [2004a,](#page-22-0) [2012)](#page-22-0) and methodological (e.g., Barad [2007,](#page-19-0) [2010;](#page-19-0) Fenwick and Edwards [2011](#page-20-0); Law [2003](#page-21-0)) alternatives to macro-analysis.
Secondly, this article addresses the way in which the Bologna Process can be conceptualised as an extensive policy borrowing process. It aims to complete the methodological ambition of studying 'smallness' and, therefore, follows up by coining the Bologna Process as a policy borrowing process. Understanding the Bologna Process as a policy borrowing process – something consisting of 'travelling reforms' – enables us to centre on local policy contexts or contextual reasons for adapting or rejecting the borrowing of international reforms.
Thirdly, this article addresses the idea that higher education reform is 'troubled' by the agency of the past. The Bologna Process has given rise to extensive curricula reform throughout Europe and beyond and, hence, this article has selected globalised curricula as its focal point. This also indicates that curriculum development and change is regarded as part of the education policy, even though it is often treated as an independent research field. The organisational effects of the globalised curricula are analysed through Derrida's neologism 'hauntology': a teaching on 'what is haunting' that enables us to understand the constitutive power of the past. In other words, it helps us to appreciate how certain aspects that appear to be excluded by current reforms continue to have a constitutive impact on what is practiced. This analysis also takes inspiration from Fenwick and Edward's notion of multiple reals and Barad's notion of entanglement and time, highlighting the ontological character of the separated practices and the idea that the past is continuously reconfigured and reshaped and, therefore, very much alive. In this sense, the agency of the past 'troubles' the present higher education reforms. Following this, the article addresses how ongoing reforms tend to increase the stretch between 'what is performed on the outside' and 'what is practiced on the inside'.
As the opening quotation by Elena tells us, the Bologna Process changes everything for those working in higher education; their way of being education, being colleagues, their relations with management and their culture. In order to understand whether and how Elena's experience of the Bologna Process as life-altering is related to globalising processes, we first need to design a different conceptual language that can capture 'global smallness'.
## Looking down: a methodological take
The concept of globalisation has been subjected to an almost invisible yet comprehensive naturalisation, meaning that it is universally appealed to as an essential mode of explaining whatever is happening within the realms of politics, economics or culture. In this sense, it has become a kind of container metaphor and is very strongly debated (Held and McGrew [2007;](#page-20-0) Scholte [2008)](#page-21-0). Some would argue that globalisation indicates a homogenisation or cultural hybridisation yielding a global identity, while others emphasise globalisation as a pathway to continuous cultural renewal and diversity.
Moreover, actors from the entire political spectrum have appropriated the concept and obscured it further by making the concept serve different ideologies (Guillén [2001,](#page-20-0) 235–260; Held [2002,](#page-20-0) 305). The English term 'globalisation' was first used to denote something as 'worldwide' in 1960 (Guillén [2001,](#page-20-0) 238). However, it seems as if there is now a type of agreement that 'globalisation' indicates as a transformation of the human way of organising the world: a transformation of political, economic and cultural structures, practices and social relations. This transformation connects geographically distant societies and expands connections of political and judicial power across the world's societies and continents (Dale and Robertson [2012;](#page-19-0) Held [2002;](#page-20-0) Robertson and Dale [2008;](#page-21-0) Scholte [2005](#page-21-0)).
Globalisation has been named 'the colossal sublime' by Derrida, a kind of 'postmodern sublime', a phenomenon of transcending dimensions which breaks with all that is previous and which equals only itself (Derrida [1987,](#page-20-0) 135, [2003;](#page-20-0) Li [2000](#page-21-0), 1). Derrida addresses the phenomenon's conceptual, discursive and rhetorical character: the concept's ambition to become a 'Master word' naming the overwhelming processes framing our contemporary world (Li [2000,](#page-21-0) 9). Derrida engages critically with this totalising and universalistic claim and the tendency towards autofinality and inevitability that seems to cancel historicity and creates the impression that the rhetoric is a 'selective, performative discourse that finds what it seeks and believes what it creates' (Li [2000,](#page-21-0) 10, 34). In essence, this is a critique of what Dale and Robertson also describe as the tendency to see categories as natural and fixed. They argue that these meta assumptions have led to certain tendencies, for example, 'spatial fetishism' which is the tendency to reify and naturalise processes such as globalisation (as in 'globalisation does'), thereby locking us into atemporal and ahistorical analyses (Dale and Robertson [2012](#page-19-0), 27).
This study leaves behind the common globalisation perspective on structural changes in nation states and national economies. Instead, it concentrates on globalisation in relation to higher education and specifically in relation to policy-making and organisational processes. However, this is exactly what unsettles the research field. Derrida's critique touches upon two core methodological issues when studying globalising processes. First, it highlights an issue that exposes potential scientific disagreements within the philosophy of science: globalisation tends to become 'all encompassing' when it emerges in its substantiated form; as a noun, the overwhelming master word Globalisation encompasses everything from terror and climate change to educational systems. When used as a master word, globalisation tends to be described as an inevitable process without any specific agency attached to it. What is often missing in macro-narratives is the importance of agency in the interpretation and negotiation of policy processes and in policy effects (Rizvi and Lingard [2010,](#page-21-0) x). Furthermore, this rhetoric is nurtured by very different philosophical assumptions about 'world and life' than the ones underpinning my project,
which are assumptions that dismiss a transcendental signifier and centre on the performative notion of globalisation displayed in its active and verbal forms of globalising processes. One of the leading performativity theorists, Karen Barad, argues that the move towards performative alternatives to representationalism shifts the focus from correspondence between description and reality to practices and doings (Barad [2007,](#page-19-0) 28). Or, to put it differently, it shifts the focus to agency; how something is enacted.
Second, Derrida's critique questions the analytical approach that is usually adopted. 'Sublime' is derived from the Latin word sublimis, which means 'high', 'elevated' or 'raised'. By calling globalisation 'sublime', Derrida questions the imagining of globalisation as something 'up there' and how this imagining presses the necessity of 'looking up' in order to study it: an approach Law relates to the principles of 'romantic complexity' (Law [2003](#page-21-0)). This 'urge' to look up can be detected as being part of both the reform- and policy-supporting perspectives and the more critical perspective within the Bologna research. The policy supporting perspective reproduces the idea of top-down policy implementation (Eurydice, Bologna Follow-up Group, Trends, stocktaking and ministerial bench-marking reports, etc.; Keeling [2004)](#page-21-0). The critical perspective is often ideologically oriented and inspired by governmentality theory. This research tends to focus on how the Bologna process is marked by a neoliberal agenda (Fejes [2006,](#page-20-0) [2008](#page-20-0)). Both approaches tend to stay captivated by the 'necessity' to 'look up' preconditioning: either a 'top-down implementation' or 'regimes of governmentality' emanating from the management level or neoliberalism 'as such' (Shore and Wright [1997](#page-21-0); Staunæs [2007](#page-22-0)).
However, this article argues that, in order to study the agency dimension of globalising processes and in order to grasp globalising processes at the organisational level, one in fact needs to look down into detailed organising processes. The 'looking down' approach is derived from Law's elaboration on 'baroque complexity' – a notion inspired by Leibniz and Deleuze – which enables the researcher to identify and explore complexity in detail (Law [2003,](#page-21-0) 6). Studying globalisation by looking down challenges the idea that, in many ways, the concept of globalisation appears to be reserved for macro-structural changes. It is continuously asserted that globalisation has a tremendous impact on everyday life, and yet is it difficult for us to demonstrate the ways in which this is so if we insist that globalisation is related only to macro-structural changes and transformations. However, if we loosen globalisation from transformations at the level of the nation state and the macro-economy, the conceptual language – which is very closely connected to macro-analysis – also tends to slip from our grasp. Therefore, a different conceptual language about globalisation is called for: tools that contain methodological and theoretical sensibilities and that can enable us to capture shifts, non-linearity and global smallness.
In recent years, researchers have aimed to shake loose globalisation's evolutionary status as the latest stage of macro-narratives (Tsing [2005,](#page-22-0) 58). Researchers are currently offering performative alternatives by exploring understandings, conceptualisations and studies of globalisation that differ from macro-analysis and aim to reconceptualise the field by connecting local enactment and international policy processes. I suggest that these are analytical conceptualisations of globalisation as created, negotiated and contested processes (Rizvi and Lingard [2010](#page-21-0); Shore and Wright [1997](#page-21-0); Tsing [2000)](#page-22-0), as specific movements of policy ideas and practices (Robertson and Dale [2008;](#page-21-0) Dale and Robertson [2012](#page-21-0); Steiner-Khamsi [2004a,](#page-22-0) [2004b,](#page-22-0) [2012](#page-22-0); Rosenau [2008;](#page-21-0) Phillips [2004;](#page-21-0) Whitty [2012;](#page-22-0) Carney [2009;](#page-19-0) Cuban [1998](#page-19-0); Rizvi and Lingard [2010](#page-21-0)) or something residing between the real and the imagined (Steiner-Khamsi [2004b)](#page-22-0). I also suggest that they are methodological conceptualisations of globalising processes, policy movements and scale, propelled (mostly) by posthumanist and performativity-oriented theory, which seeks to revitalise ontological considerations, as in the case of Barad's agential realism or Fenwick and Edwards' actor-network theory (ANT)-inspired understandings of policy processes as mobilised by micro-negotiations, Rosenau's suggestion of a journalistic-inspired methodology moving from micro-incidents to more general processes, Reinhold's policy-anthropological 'studying through' perspective or Law's Leibniz and Deleuze-inspired subversion of the global to situated 'smallness' (Barad [2007;](#page-19-0) Fenwick and Edwards [2011](#page-20-0); Law [2003](#page-21-0); Rosenau [2008;](#page-21-0) Shore and Wright [1997](#page-21-0); Wright and Reinhold [2011](#page-22-0)). These approaches represent performative clarifications of globalisation and education but are connected to a wider field of poststructuralist researchers who wish to emphasise materiality and agency as important factors (Bramming [2012;](#page-19-0) Butler [1993](#page-19-0); Haraway [1991](#page-20-0); Juelskjær [2013](#page-20-0); Juelskjær, Staunæs, and Ratner [2013;](#page-21-0) Mol [2002;](#page-21-0) Staunæs [2007](#page-22-0); Søndergaard [2013)](#page-22-0). In various ways, these approaches tend to relinquish the imagining of global as macro and local as micro. Also, as Robertson suggests, they attempt to challenge the exclusive interpretation of the global as scale, primarily connoting size, and broaden it with understandings of the global as reach, connoting impact (Robertson et al. [2012)](#page-21-0). Macro-narratives constrain our analytic imagination. However, leaving them aside confronts us with a formidable challenge, since many of the present analytical concepts focus almost exclusively on macro-phenomena (Rosenau [2008)](#page-21-0).
## Policy borrowing
According to Rizvi and Lingard, 'globalisation cannot be viewed as a generalised phenomenon but rather needs to be seen as a dynamic phenomenon expressed in particular histories and political configurations' (Rizvi and Lingard [2010,](#page-21-0) x). For them, policy is both product and process. They reject one-way and linear accounts of the policy process as something that emanates
from the setting of political agendas, the production of the policy text and its implementation into practice. Instead, they emphasise the messy, contested and non-linear relationships that exist between the various negotiation zones in the policy process. The participating actors are not simply passive receptacles (Rizvi and Lingard [2010](#page-21-0), 5, 6). Despite what we might call new global conditions, Rizvi and Lingard argue against treating global processes as historically inevitable: as processes that people and nations simply have to come to terms with.
Policy borrowing and lending, policy transfer, policy mobility, policy travel, policy movement, policy attraction and policy tourism are all terms that aim to describe the movement of policy ideas and practices, including those concerned with higher education (Dale and Robertson [2012](#page-19-0); Steiner-Khamsi [2004a,](#page-22-0) [2012)](#page-22-0). Policy borrowing, understood not only as a research field but also as a research approach, offers a way to operationalise the tracing of globalising processes as specific agencies at the organisational and individual level. Or, in other words, it offers a conceptual framework for studying crossnational policy attraction, including the relation between situated events and international dynamics (Carney [2009,](#page-19-0) 63; Phillips [2004](#page-21-0)). Rather than focusing on macro-phenomena, researchers engaged with travelling reforms centre on local policy contexts or contextual reasons for adapting or rejecting the borrowing of international reforms. Alongside this, several other commentators, such as Dale and Robertson [(2012](#page-19-0)), Marsh and Sharman [(2009](#page-21-0)) and Steiner-Khamsi, highlight the agency dimension of studying policy transfer processes: 'Emphasis on local policy context as the analytical unit for examining policy transfer places greater weight on the agency, process, impact, and timing of policy borrowing' (Steiner-Khamsi [2012,](#page-22-0) 5). In this way, a policy borrowing perspective differs from perspectives reproducing the understanding of reforms as inevitable and approaching from the 'outside' or 'up there', as outlined in the previous section. Keeling [(2004](#page-21-0)) also identifies that research on the very enactment of policy processes within educational organisations seems to be lacking. This is probably due, in part, to the somewhat tenacious maintenance of globalised processes belonging exclusively to the macro-structural level (as indicated previously, this approach provides no language to capture the shifting 'reals' at the organisational level), but it is also due to the way in which policy formation is conceived; often based on the assumption that policy analysis involves studying rational and linear decision-making processes. The multilayered Bologna Process clearly shows that there is much more involved.
Due to profound international reforms, we are facing an increasing need to explore international educational spaces, such as the Bologna Process, in higher education; not just as a macro phenomenon, but also as an educational space that includes the agencies at the organisational and individual level (Dale and Robertson [2012](#page-19-0); Steiner-Khamsi [2012](#page-22-0)).
## The loose ends of the Bologna Process
The Bologna Process is based on the Bologna Declaration, which had been ratified by 47 nations by the time of the launching of the European Higher Education Area in 2010 (EHEA-Ministers [2010)](#page-20-0). The Bologna Process cannot be regarded as one coherent narrative nor as a consistent and harmonic phenomenon (Keeling [2004](#page-21-0)). The European Higher Education Area has no single 'centre', rather it appears as though the European educational organisations are asymmetrically related to each other, leaving the so-called Bologna Process to be a relatively open frame of reference, suggesting that processes like Bologna have provided a welcome opportunity to justify and accelerate domestic educational reforms (Ravinet [2008](#page-21-0); Steiner-Khamsi [2004b](#page-22-0)). One may even say that the European Higher Education Area functions as a regulatory ideal (Nóvoa and Lawn [2002](#page-21-0)) and, thus, in a certain way, a blind reference. Of course, this condition – that there seems to be no tidy edges to these fragmented processes – complicates the empirical examination of the Bologna Process and exposes major theoretical and methodological challenges. Furthermore, there is no legislative power connected to the process and it has therefore been actualised at different paces due to the so-called open method of coordination (OMC), which is based on voluntariness and the assigning of greater priority to benchmarking and local best practice (Dale [2004;](#page-19-0) Gornitzka [2005](#page-20-0); Henckel and Wright [2008;](#page-20-0) Keeling [2006](#page-21-0)). The OMC works by individual countries implementing the concepts and ideas within national laws and regulations. Because of the collective pressure and the profound incentive structures, it does not seem a realistic option to remain outside the OMC framework. 'Soft' technologies, like the OMC, can be hardcore performative (Dean [2007)](#page-20-0). The continuous transformation of the Bologna incitement structures appears as a convincing example. From its informal and flexible beginnings, the process has slid towards more unified and formal constraints that have proved very binding for the signatory states (Ravinet [2008)](#page-21-0). This is displayed most powerfully through the development of the follow-up mechanisms applied during the process. Ravinet [(2008](#page-21-0)) identifies this process as a movement from 'voluntary participation' to 'monitored coordination'. Some of the disciplining technologies used to evaluate the implementation of the Bologna objectives are national reports, the Trends reports from the European University Association (EUA), stocktaking reports and the The Bologna Follow-up Group (BFUG). At the outset, national reports are voluntary, but they soon become binding and are followed by demands of extensive standardisation that make it easier to perform comparisons between participating countries. This is combined with the increased use of colourcoded scorecards [dark green for 'excellent performance', light green for 'very good' and, from here, on to red, indicating that 'little progress has been made yet', as can be seen in the stocktaking reports (BFUG-Stocktaking-Working-Group [2005](#page-19-0), 15)]. These technologies lead to performative effects by creating
'incitement' through competition and 'naming and shaming' mechanisms, as Ravinet ([2008)](#page-21-0) so clearly documents. The potential embarrassment of failure adds enormous pressure and this, in turn, propels the implementation process (Ravinet [2008,](#page-21-0) 362). The intensification of the organising management technologies also correlates with the increased entanglement with the European competitive (growth) strategies as such. Already in the Bologna declaration in 1999, promises are made to increase the international competitiveness of the European system of higher education. In 2007, European ministers adopted the Strategy for the European Higher Education Area in a Global Setting, which was designed to enhance competitiveness. Together with the EU's growth strategy, Europe 2020, the strategy constitutes part of the Higher Education Modernisation Agenda, published in 2011 (EHEA-Ministers [2007;](#page-20-0) European Commission [2010](#page-20-0), [2011](#page-20-0)). These strategies portray higher education as a strong driver of economic growth. In 1999, there was no way of predicting the 'future proportions' of the Bologna Process or of anticipating its effects, especially its unintended effects such as the dismantling of the constitutive organising principles at higher education institutions, the intense battling between lecturers, and the emergence of shadow practicing (which will be examined in the following sections).
Since the Bologna Process operates with very effective follow-up technologies, despite its fragmented character, the globalising of the Bologna Process is possibly one of the most extensive examples of policy transfer in higher education (Dale and Robertson [2012](#page-19-0); Steiner-Khamsi [2012)](#page-22-0). The Bologna ambitions have given rise to extensive curricula reform throughout Europe and beyond: flows of educational policies and practices also named consumerist mechanisms by Naidoo ([2003](#page-21-0); Naidoo, Shankar, and Veer [2011](#page-21-0)). These reforms include shifts from semestrial time-frame structures to modular structures, in which each module constitutes a learning unit in itself and must be completed by a test. They also implicate shifts in orientation, from curricula oriented towards the student's development throughout his/her education to curricula oriented towards learning outcomes; knowledge, skills and competence, as identified by the the European Qualification Frameworks (EQF) (EHEA-Ministers [2001,](#page-20-0) [2005](#page-20-0); European Commission [2008](#page-20-0)). The core of the EQF concerns eight reference levels, which describe what a learner knows, understands and is able to do on completion of a learning process. The Danish qualification framework follows the European framework with regard to the learning outcomes, and these learning outcomes are put to work in new educational ministerial orders and curricula. The entire process has altered what it means to talk about knowledge and educational organisation and, through this, it has also changed what is sayable, doable and probably even bodyable as an actor taking part in the organising processes. However, the empirical data informing this article suggest that it may have changed in unexpected ways. It seems as though the collapse of past and present leads to
unforeseen consequences. In order to detect what moves and shifts the 'reals' at the organisational level, we need an analytical tool that can help us display the constitutive powers.
## Hauntology
The philosophical concept of hauntology expresses a way of thinking that enables us to understand the ways in which the reform processes are haunted by what is seemingly absent. This analytical approach also relates to the manner in which the ethnographic method employed here allows us to gain access to what is not immediately visible: gaining access to what 'is not there'. In this sense, ethnography becomes a kind of 'ethnography of absence': a tool to explore the constitutive effects of what is supposedly absent:
As in Hamlet, the Prince of a rotten state, everything begins with the apparition of a specter. (Derrida [1994,](#page-20-0) 2)
In Specters of Marx from 1994, Derrida starts developing his concept on ghosts by creating a neologism, the so-called 'hauntology': a 'teaching on what is haunting'. Hauntology is a near homophone to ontology in French. Whereas ontology is the teaching on what exists, a teaching on the Da-sein, the being-there, hauntology is a teaching on what is not being-there (Derrida [1994,](#page-20-0) 202). In a way, hauntology is a supplement to ontology, and we have learned from Derrida's work that the constitutive power tends to be imbedded in the supplement, 'the rest', the margins or what is seemingly 'absent'. Ghosts are half-lives. They are an undetectable passage between loci and time, and are able to collapse past and present. According to Derrida, there is no Da-sein of the spectre. But neither is there Da-sein without the uncanniness (Unheimlichkeit) of some spectre. In a way, ghosts are 'absence' with agency (Brøgger [2013;](#page-19-0) Brøgger and Staunæs [2012](#page-19-0)). What is absent will always 'disturb'. It is beyond being but it appears and it haunts. The ghost is a revenant: it returns, 'it ghosts', it 'specters', as Derrida [(1994](#page-20-0), 10, 166) says:
A question of repetition: a specter is always a revenant. One cannot control its comings and goings because it begins by coming back. (Derrida [1994](#page-20-0), 11)
Introducing the concept of hauntology in these studies allows us to present both a philosophical and an empirical point. The philosophical insight emphasises that ghosts first and foremost haunt Da-sein or ontology pure and simple: the idea that we can freeze ontological stands or centre on a single, hegemonic ontology. This insight connects with the empirical material; on the one hand, it appears as though the reform processes are haunted by what is seemingly absent; that the change in the organisation is propelled by something returning from absence (namely, as we shall see in this case, the
old disciplinary groups). On the other hand, it is quite impossible to identify 'the reality' of the organisation; instead, various 'reals' seem to be evoked.
### Multiple and entangled 'reals'
Fenwick and Edwards perform an ANT-inspired reconceptualisation of policy processes (Fenwick and Edwards [2011](#page-20-0)) that is very closely related to Barad's diffractive methodology, which she presents in her major work from 2007, Meeting the Universe Halfway. Enrolled in previous poststructuralist innovations (e.g., Haraway and Mol), Fenwick and Edwards introduce materiality into educational research. Though Barad derives her ideas from quantum physics (Niels Bohr), continental philosophy (Foucault and Derrida) and queer studies (Haraway and Butler), Fenwick, Edwards and Barad meet in a mutual interest to revitalise the status of ontology or simply materiality in poststructuralist thinking. Whereas Barad introduces an onto-epistemological framework, the so-called agential realism, and thereby situates her work as a profound subversion of representationalism (Barad [2007,](#page-19-0) 44), Fenwick and Edwards choose to oppose constructivism. They criticise the idea that constructivism merely offers different perspectives on a world which is indirectly and often inadvertently assumed to be there. Fenwick and Edwards argue that diversity is not produced by multiple perspectives, but that we are in fact part of different 'worlds', or 'reals' that coexist and overlap, 'patched together in the same material spaces' (Fenwick and Edwards [2011,](#page-20-0) 710, 722). Studying these overlapping ontologies would, according to Fenwick and Edwards, mean observing the proliferation of practices and meanings as different worlds, not just different world views (Fenwick and Edwards [2011,](#page-20-0) 722). This means that policy becomes a question of 'the fragile enrolments of multiple ontologies rather than the stable transcendence into a single ontology' and policy enactments 'a patching together of different realities' (Fenwick and Edwards [2011,](#page-20-0) 723).
By taking multiple ontologies as a point of departure, it is possible to show the ontological variance in educational policy enactments and the practices through which different policy actors negotiate these multiplicities (Fenwick and Edwards [2011,](#page-20-0) 724). This basically means exploring how agency is distributed and how certain accounts of it fix and dissolve in temporary stabilisations (Fenwick and Edwards [2011,](#page-20-0) 721). These stabilisations relate to Barad's agential cuts (Barad [2007](#page-19-0), 345, 347). Specific material practices – apparatuses – enact a so-called agential cut. According to Barad, who draws upon Butler's notion of performativity as a reiterative and citational practice, apparatuses are boundary-drawing open-ended practices, dynamic and iterative reconfigurings of the world (Barad [2007](#page-19-0), 167, 184, 208; Butler [1993](#page-19-0), 2). Each cut, the way something is read or examined, evokes a different 'world' or, more precisely, each cut constitutes a dynamic reconfiguring of the world. This basically changes the perception of ontology from entities in traditional
metaphysics to entangled ontology. In traditional metaphysics, epistemology and ontology are separate and are considered as binary oppositions: a position that is maintained from classical positivism to critical realism. In Barad's thinking, one cannot meaningfully distinguish between epistemology and ontology; there is only onto-epistemology. And, perhaps most importantly, classical metaphysics is all about finding accurate representations. However, Barad highlights another approach which emphasises that different practices matter; that the world simply materialises differently through different practices (Barad [2007](#page-19-0), 89).
#### The agency of ghosts
Enter the ghost, exit the ghost […] (Hamlet) […]. (Derrida [1994](#page-20-0), xix)
Karen sees two lecturers approaching her. They are from another disciplinary group. They are moving fast, determined, and with great precision. She's about to enter an office but they catch her in the doorway. They corner her and hold her up with their weapons (the ministerial order and the first drafts of the curriculum). Starring at her, they demand her to give up some ECTS points from her group to theirs. Can't she see that it's only fair? The content linked to these ECTS points rightfully belongs to them. They have always covered that area, they argue. She's new, she doesn't know how to react, and what this is. She's never been cornered like this before. She tries to get away, but they keep arguing and trying to convince her. Finally, she escapes into the office.
Chris, another lecturer, says during an interview:
This has become everybody fighting everybody […] It seems as if there are small juntas showing up everywhere […] I've never been so alert before in my life.
The new ministerial orders and curricula shaped in accordance with the European reform processes have profound effects, since they cause reorganisations of work distribution and shifts in positions. When studying the empirical material, two curricular shifts stand out in particular:
- . The shift from a semestrial to a modular structure, in which modules are divided into a number of European Credit Transfer System (ECTS) points (ECTS serves as a common European standard enabling the measurement of workload and recognition of studies abroad) and must be individually tested. This shift also indicates a shift from subject-based teaching to transdisciplinary teaching. - . The shift from organising the education according to subject areas to organising the education according to the so-called core areas, which are thematically determined and not shaped by any specific subject. Each core area has its own defined learning outcomes. The modules follow the
core areas and hence the students must be tested within the core areas and not in subject areas.
Previously, the constitutive organising of work revolved around so-called disciplinary groups, which were linked to subject areas. However, as part of the new organising model, lecturers are now divided into transdisciplinary teams that follow the core areas and the development of each module. These teams have the responsibility of both teaching and developing the content of the modules assigned to them. This manoeuvre – the reorganising of the work in accordance with the implementation of the new education – has resulted in the dismantling of the most constitutive and powerful organising principle among the lecturers. Previously, the disciplinary groups were very strongly positioned within the educational organisation and protected not only the interests of their discipline but also the interests of lecturers against management in general (in their own view). Lecturers refer to this group as 'home', 'family' or 'backing group'. The disciplinary groups are now marginalised, partly due to the new organisational principle – it is the responsibility of the teams, and not the disciplinary groups, to run the modules – and partly due to the fact that they are eliminated from the ministerial order and the curriculum.
As we have just seen, lecturers are currently fighting over the distribution of ECTS points. Although it may seem surprising, a lot is at stake here. ECTS points are distributed in accordance with the size of modules; however, when developing the content of these modules in teams, each participant in the transdisciplinary team still acts as if they were representing their old disciplinary group, and the development of the module partly turns into a negotiation on ECTS points related to the old subject areas. This process causes some lecturers to lose organisational 'volume': they simply become smaller and they 'hold' a smaller part of the education as a whole. The old disciplinary groups are slain and, in this sense, they are dead, absent. Yet they also seem very much alive, however ghostly their manner, and start hunting down colleagues in the corridors or policing the dialogue between the lecturers.
Enter the ghost, exit the ghost, re-enter the ghost (Hamlet) […]. (Derrida [1994](#page-20-0), xix)
The disciplinary groups reenter the scene. It is late afternoon and lecturers gather at a team meeting. Their task is to develop one of the modules for the new curriculum. They represent different academic backgrounds. They all understand themselves as delegates acting on behalf of their old disciplinary groups; when they refer to 'us', it is always the 'backing group'. They discuss the content of the module. The working paper they have before them currently consists of bullet points containing different aspects of the knowledge required. They continue, as they politely discuss which areas belong to which disciplinary groups:
One of the lecturers, Anne, states that, as she sees it, psychology, organisation and culture overlap. Another lecturer, Vinnie, interrupts, leans forward and says, 'I really think it would be great if you psychologists could provide the students with hard core knowledge on the psychological dimensions and then we as social scientists could teach culture. I often think they lack hard core psychology and this is so important to their future job and also you are so good at doing this'. Anne says; let me give you an example; Schein is also a big name within psychology, we use him as well as you do. Another lecturer, Jacob, says. 'Oh I thought he was ours'.
The reorganising dislocates positions and transforms marginal positions into dominant ones. Some stand to lose organisational volume, and some stand to reclaim or gain volume. As the previous observation shows, it seems as if the lecturers appreciate each other's disciplines, yet, at the same time, and in a very subtle manner, they imperialise new areas, like when Vinnie commends Anne for being so good at teaching that part of her discipline does not extend into Vinnie's own field. It is not possible for the lecturers to claim their discipline as they used to. They have to defend their 'turf' in various ways or exploit the possibility of conquering new territory. Vinnie continues:
But of course we can figure something out, you know, something that makes sense to the students. They know nothing worse than when things are repeated. You know the scenario; you enter class and introduce the subject and they all yell, 'We've already covered that!'. But, of course, we can figure something out.
Vinnie, who is still very appreciative and forthcoming, now conquers the view of the students and is therefore able to emphasise that she only wishes to protect their interests. The meeting continues in a similar fashion: a fight to monopolise areas however subtle and polite the manner. However, the document they need to deliver cannot contain these subject areas. It must only outline the content of the module and not divide it into different subject areas. Constantly, engaging in the fight over subject areas, they quickly agree that they need at least two documents: an official one, outlining the content of the module as required by the ministerial order, and another, unofficial one, which divides the content into the old subject areas.
The old disciplinary groups have been slain and as a result of the new ministerial order and curriculum, they have been excluded. However, returning from the dead to haunt the living, the old disciplinary groups fuel the actions of the lecturers. In the shape of small ghost armies, juntas, they start hunting down colleagues in the corridor, only to return and start policing the dialogue between the lecturers negotiating the content of the module. In this way, they start collapsing past and present, providing what seems to be absent with constitutive power. And this cannot be reduced to a question of different worldviews; they literally perform different practices and thereby evoke different worlds with very material and 'real' effects for everyday organisational life and, not least, of course, for educational practice.
Ghosts have agency: the past is provided with agency through historical ways of organising workloads or budgets. The lecturers' actions – their hunting each other down in the corridors and their subtle negotiations and creation of 'shadow documents' – are propelled by the agency of a past that is never closed (Barad [2007](#page-19-0), 383, [2010](#page-19-0), 264). According to Barad, who is also inspired by Derrida's hauntology, the past is iteratively reworked and reconfigured. The past was never simply there to begin with (Barad [2007,](#page-19-0) 315–316). Phenomena are not located in space and time, they are constituted by entanglements extending across spaces and times and they are iteratively reconfigured through the ongoing intra-activity of the world (Barad [2007](#page-19-0), 376). Past and present collapse and the past is reconfigured in specific ways propelled by the present reform processes. The past is reconfigured in new ways because of the collapse with the present. The lecturers' different ways of 'doing' education is not what the original political agendas set out to realise, but it is also different from what they used to do, and they do not necessarily do the same (Brøgger [2013](#page-19-0)). The ministerial orders have performative effects and push the lecturers in unintended ways. They start imperialising, sometimes through the subtle containment of new area, like Vinnie commending Anne, and sometimes in open battle, like Karen being cornered by a 'junta'.
## Give to the emperor
The lecturers' conclusion in their meeting emphasises the ghostly character; the lecturers are producing 'shadow documents' behind the official ones – shadow documents that guide their practice. They actively produce different worlds and different practices that add to and shape the practice in the organisation. What is also interesting is that it seems as if the lecturers share this 'phantom behaviour' with management, since their acting is haunted by the past and is taking place behind the official organising and officials documents. As part of the ongoing reform processes, new tools and standards are implemented in relation to quality assurance and new ways of documenting the use of economic resources in general. Part of this concerns the question of how to register different activities regarding administration, teaching and research, etc. Universities and university colleges have to account for their financial expenditure. Their budgets and accounts are still very much connected to their previous (smaller and more independent) institutions – before extensive mergers and institutional standardisations took place – and, therefore, do not correspond to the common standards. This obviously constitutes a profound challenge when having to meet new demands:
At a meeting, they discuss the difficulties and challenges connected to the ministerial demands on what percentage of the overall economy of the organisation that should go to administration, and what percentage to teaching. They are struggling to understand the logics of the new requirements for budgets
and accounting. They discuss that it is difficult to meet the percentages, especially the demands on how much should be allocated to teaching. They argue that a lot of things can be regarded as teaching and learning, including the student's own study time. They relate this argument to the idea of the so called 'student centred learning'. The new requirements collide with the old systems and, therefore, one of the managers now states that they 'can easily move the numbers to the 'politically correct columns' [columns for resources spend on teaching] if necessary and for the occasion'.
By performing a certain 'phantom behaviour', lecturers and management offer the emperor those items that are his. However, behind this, as they produce documents or move numbers from one column to another, they enact very different ways of 'doing' their work. The moment you change numbers or fabricate yet another shadow document, a different world is evoked. Lecturers and management are not merely adding different perspectives to the same reality. They are rather doing the education and doing the numbers in different ways and thereby evoking different worlds. The numbers and documents have very performative effects in that they enact the organisation and the educations in different ways. Different practices matter, as Barad states – both in the sense of carrying significance and carrying materiality (and producing material effects). Each 'world' is ghostly in the sense that it does not 'hold' a strong ontology; the multiple ghostly ontologies are fragile, 'weak' ontologies; they are each a dynamic reconfiguring of the world – they are rolling, they shift and change in the moment you switch the numbers or produce a document. Each 'world' is a temporary stabilisation. Each agential cut – a document produced or numbers moved to a different column – enacts a 'world'. This is also what Barad calls worlding, the continuous creation of referentiality. For Barad, this is the case precisely because agency is not an attribute. It is not something that someone or something has; rather, it is the ongoing reconfigurings of the world. Policy enactment then becomes a patching together of different realities (in the same material spaces), as Fenwick and Edwards argue (Fenwick and Edwards [2011,](#page-20-0) 710). The educational agents do not simply cope as passive receptacles of the reform. Instead, they adopt some parts and reject others. Cuban and Steiner-Khamsi argue that schools change reforms as much as reforms change schools (Cuban [1998](#page-19-0); Steiner-Khamsi [2012)](#page-22-0). Looking at the practices of both lecturers and managers certainly suggests that higher education consists currently of multiple educational realities, but the 'successful implementation' of the Bologna standards conceals this somewhat messier picture. The 'phantom behaviour', including the battling of the ghostly worlds, the haunting of the past and the ghostly documents and columns, also gives this impression. Nathaniel, a lecturer, confirms the lecturers' 'phantom behaviour' as he describes the implementation process:
It has caused utter chaos and the only way we can handle it is by double entry bookkeeping.
Nathaniel uses the double-entry bookkeeping figuratively to address their double strategy. It is logics stemming from the old disciplinary groups that propel the development of the curriculum; however, before publishing the curriculum, Nathaniel says, they produce a format confirming, on paper, that the new core areas are taken into account:
It's a complete mystery to us how these 'core areas' came up in the first place […] They simply don't exist as something people can identify with […] We have created something we call 'securing of the core areas' […] The core areas don't work as a guiding principle … how should I put this … they don't 'govern' or 'steer' anything.
The new organising – exemplified here by Nathaniel through a description of the core areas – may not act as a guiding principle for the lecturers. However, this does not mean that they are not governed by these changes. Meanwhile, as we have learned, a phenomenon – for instance, (the continuous negotiation and contestation of) education reform – is constituted by entanglements extending across spaces (from European ministers negotiating a modular structure to lecturers developing a module) and times (as the reconfigured past in the shape of, for instance, 'juntas' enter and change the present). This extensive understanding of an unfolding historicity breaks the illusion of linearity. As the past and present collapse, the reforms produce profound performative effects that were unforeseen by policy-makers and the educational agents themselves – like the subtle imperialising through containment of new area, the fierce imperialising through the intense battling of the juntas, the production of shadow documents or the exercising of match-making between numbers and columns. In this sense, the reforms are indeed governing – but, as they govern, new ontologies are evoked witnessing the existence of alternative educational realities and thereby also turning everything into negotiables. One of the mid-level managers reflects on the implementation process:
The most important management task used to belong to these groups [the old disciplinary groups]: How do we manage and divide labour? How do we define our assignment? […] The old disciplinary groups are a direct manifestation of power structures […] Just the fact that as a boss I have to negotiate the managerial rights … well that's just … […] There is a very, how should I put this, an unstated but yet very strong separation of powers [among the lecturers] […] You [indicating both lecturers and management] don't mess with … the bastions of power.
That is also why Elena (in the opening quotation) can say that the reforms change and affect everything: lecturers, management, their culture and their way of being education. It is an ontological collision, overlapping but also competing practices, among the lecturers and between the lecturers and management, perpetually producing and reconfiguring educational realities. It
is a collision constantly juggled in the present, which makes organisational realities and the 'imagined implementation' of reforms so very complex.
## Eat the document: conclusion
This article has shown that the implementation of a globalised curriculum shaped in correspondence with the European reform processes pushes and reorganises educational work. What seems to be excluded and 'referred to absence' returns to haunt the living and, thereby, emerges as a constitutive power in terms of co-shaping everyday work-life and educational practice. However, as the past and present collapse, educational practices differing from both previous practice and political agendas emerge.
Of course, the global is vision, just like in the Bologna Process's desire for 'worldwide attractiveness' (EHEA-Ministers [2007](#page-20-0)) and it is text in terms of new laws and regulation that shapes the curriculum (to name but one example). But it is also local negotiation and enactment (Carney [2009,](#page-19-0) 67) propelled by very different considerations and agendas displaying, what could be called, global smallness. Global smallness differs considerably from the new imaginative regimes of global competitiveness, which are desired in the official documents of the Bologna Process (EHEA-Ministers [2007](#page-20-0)). Negotiations and contestations across spaces and times break the illusion of reform as linear and rational decision-making, frictionlessly emanating down through the organisation leading to calculated changes of practice. Rather it is suggested that globalised reform processes, such as the Bologna Process, is not one reality given from the 'outside', but consists of multiple 'reals' that 'trouble' the ongoing reforms. This indicates that the Bologna Process is more than the declarations, the communiqués and ministerial orders, but is a phenomenon continuously being 'performed', reshaped, expanded and changed through negotiations between these multiplicities of worlds – and reconfigurings of times as the past and present collapse. This article has shown that the agency of the reform is distributed and that each world, evoked from different negotiating positions, is a 'plea bargaining' in which the reform fixes and dissolves in temporary stabilisations.
The global is not just a question of scale, but also of reach, and it reaches far into the everyday practices of higher education. It changes everything, as Elena said in the introduction, but, as we have seen, not necessarily in ways we would expect. The reforms' performative effects extend far beyond what was initially anticipated. The empirical data suggests that pressure from the ongoing globalised reforms adds to the intensification of the stretch between 'what is performed on the outside' and 'what is practiced on the inside': the distance displayed through the double-entry bookkeeping logic, lecturers producing shadow documents behind the official ones and managers moving numbers between columns. The educational agents seem to enact differing 'reals' behind the exterior performance. Therefore, in order to explore global
smallness, it seems that one needs to look down and look behind the official organisings and documents and trace what is not there: the ghosts of higher education reform.
